Tier — for your PC

Shadows
Bloom / flare
Depth of field

Lower tiers render at a lower resolution with smaller or no shadow maps and fewer post effects, so weaker PCs stay smooth; High and Ultra give the full cinematic PBR look. The toggles fine-tune the tier — changing tier resets them to that tier's defaults.

Focus follows the camera target — whatever you orbit around stays sharp.

These drive the depth of field: it needs the Graphics section's Depth of field toggle on and a perspective camera (Free / Isometric) — the flat Front / Top / Left / Right elevations stay sharp. Pick a point on the wall and it stays in focus while you move the camera; a wide aperture (f/1.4) with more bokeh melts the rest of the stage away, f/16 keeps nearly everything sharp.

Visual
Speed — 100%

Start your composition in Resolume Arena, press this button and pick the Resolume window (or the screen showing its output) in the browser's share picker. The picture is mapped across the virtual wall so you can VJ against your layout — a simulation in this tab only; for a real show, Resolume still outputs to the processor as usual.

Sources stay in this browser tab — nothing is sent anywhere, and the simulator source isn't saved into the layout JSON (per-session). Cabinets you cut out with Shape edit stay empty — no cabinet and no black fill there — just like the plain 3D view.

Fit

The simulator runs only here, in the Render view — leaving Render switches it off, and the 2D layout and the normal 3D view stay clean mapping views. If a display shows the wrong slice of the picture, the source's size doesn't match the layout's total resolution — open Window → Data & Stats for the exact size and set your Resolume composition (or render) to that size.

3D couldn't start

The 3D library (three.js) didn't load — check your connection, then reopen the 3D view. Your 2D layout is unaffected.

PIVOTCentre · 50%

Bending never changes panel count, resolution, ports or cabling — only the shape on stage. The pivot is the point the wall bends around — drag the amber diamond on the wall in the 2D view, or the amber ball in the 3D Edit view, to move it. These are the same settings as the Bend tool window, so the two stay in step.

View mode is look-only. In Edit mode, drag a display on the floor — sideways syncs to the 2D layout; forward / back is depth (Z), 3D-only. The floor is height 0 — nothing can go below it.

The camera icons are view cubes, like 3ds Max and Blender — the solid face is the side you look from. Front / Top / Left / Right are flat orthographic views. Free is the full camera — drag to orbit, right-drag to pan, scroll to zoom.

Shaded shows each screen in its chosen colour, as a colour / lighter-colour chessboard like the 2D view. Flat turns the walls into a signal / port map — every cabinet in its flat port colour with its port number — and draws the rest of the stage in flat tones. Wireframe draws edges only. View modes only; they never change the layout. For a finished picture, press Render next to 3D View in the top bar.

Not connected

Independent (the default) — not connected: positions and facings are fully separate. Moving or rotating a wall in 3D changes only the 3D stage, and 2D edits never rearrange where a wall stands in 3D — but a screen's SIZE is shared both ways: scaling a wall in 3D, scaling it in 2D, or setting Columns / Rows in the Screens tab resizes it in both views, and panel count, resolution and ports follow. The 2D layout stays the source of truth for cabling, ports and the PNG — so an arena 360 preset stays a long strip in 2D and a ring in 3D, at the same size in both.

Add a modifier to the stage

Export

Media server mapping

Arena Layout — a Resolume Arena Advanced Output screensetup (.xml): one slice per screen, drawn exactly as the screens sit in the 2D view, at the layout's exact pixel size. Set the composition to that size, then load the preset in Advanced Output. Arena Video Slices — the same layout as a clean Resolume Arena 7.6 XmlState ScreenSetup (.xml): one video slice per screen, in layout order (left-to-right, top-to-bottom), each slice's InputRect and OutputRect set to that screen's rectangle on the canvas. Set the composition to the layout's pixel size, then load the file in Advanced Output.

Technical

The whole stage as a 3D model, in metres: every cabinet an extruded box with its port colour on the front face, including bends, stacking, depth (Z) and preview tilts, plus the stage deck — and the truss system and the lights export too, each as its own named part, so the model carries the whole rig, not the walls only. Every format also carries a UV map of the front faces spanning the whole 2D layout — the layout is the UV map — so content made to the layout's pixel size (or your exported PNG's layout area) drops straight onto the walls in Blender, Twinmotion, Cinema 4D or Unreal. FBX is written in centimetres (the FBX standard unit) as an ASCII file.

Signal Panel

Signal routing for the selected display — where its feed starts, the cable path through its cabinets, and how data ports split. Changes apply to the layout, cabling list and exports straight away.

Cabinets / port
Pixels / port

655,360 px is the common NovaStar / Colorlight loading limit for one Ethernet port at 60 Hz. Port numbers continue across displays — Screen 1 might use ports 1–5, Screen 2 continues at port 6 — so one processor patch list covers the whole layout.

Preferences

General

Layout & interface settings for the whole app. Preferences are saved with your layout (File → Save layout) and restored when you load it.

The unit used by every measurement in the app: the Transform panel (Location and Scale width / height — Rotation stays in degrees), every width / height field (screens, cabinet size, deck, truss, lights, props, stage pieces), the Measurements display (the ruler toggle — dimension lines in the 2D view and on every element of the 3D stage), the truss measurements, the human height label, the Cabinet Detail strip, the stats, the spec sheet and the Technical Document PDF. Internal values stay in metres — only the numbers you read and type convert. Change it here and everything updates at once.

Stage title chipProject name and layout summary at the top-left of the canvas.
Port legendThe colour key for ports along the bottom of the canvas.
Cabinet detail stripThe bar under the canvas — present in the 2D, 3D and Render views — that carries the selected screen's information (name, size, resolution, cabinets, ports) and, when a cabinet is inspected, its number, port and position.
Canvas dot gridThe dotted background grid on the stage canvas.

Learning modeShow the additional information — guidance hints, explanations and how-to notes — across the panels and the canvas. Off by default, for a clean interface.

Keyboard shortcuts

The layout works from the keyboard too. To change a shortcut, click its key button and press the new key combination — Esc cancels. If the combination already belongs to another shortcut, that one is cleared. Shortcuts are saved with your layout (File → Save layout), like the other preferences.

Screens overlap

Screen 2 overlaps Screen 1 in the 2D layout. Is this overlap OK?

In the 2D layout screens should sit side by side without overlapping — two screens on the same stage area usually means a placement mistake. Confirm only if you really want them to overlap.

Link the layouts?

Linked connects the two layouts into one shared layout.

Independent keeps the two layouts fully separate — the 2D strip stays exactly as drawn (the source of truth for cabling, ports and the PNG export) while the 3D stage arranges the same walls its own way. That is why arena, cube, bent and stacked layouts stay Independent.

Magnet strength
15° · 10 px

How hard the magnet pulls while snap is on (or Shift is held): weak 5° / 0.05 m · medium 15° / 0.10 m · strong 30° / 0.25 m · max 45° / 0.50 m. In the 3D view it snaps the moves and turns of screens, truss segments, lights and props to those steps; in 2D it snaps gizmo drags to the matching pixel grid (5 / 10 / 25 / 50 px).

Bending never changes panel count, resolution, ports or cabling — only the shape on stage. The 2D view stays the accurate flat front elevation: its width is the wall's true surface length (the arc length for soft modules); the curved footprint shows in the 3D view. Soft modules bend along one axis only, like rolling a sheet — never across the rows.
